passage: In Jamal's room in Nairobi, the guitar case wore a soft coat of dust. Jin, who had come over to borrow a charger, looked at it, then at the laptop still open at lesson four of an online coding course, then at the running shoes by the door. “Three things,” Jin said. “None finished.” Jamal shrugged. “The next one will be different.” He pulled up a video about making music on a laptop and his eyes lit up, exactly as they had for the guitar. Jin didn't say anything. Later, walking home, Jamal caught himself thinking that he always started well and never got to the end, and it felt oddly like a fact about himself.

qa.q: At which lesson was the coding course left?
qa.a: The coding course was left at lesson four.

qa.q: Why did Jamal's eyes light up at the music video?
qa.a: Jamal felt fresh excitement, the same as he felt for the guitar, because a new idea is more thrilling than pushing an old one through its dull stretch.

qa.q: What could Jamal try before starting the music idea?
qa.a: Choose one of the three older projects, do a small piece of it each day for two weeks, and only then decide about the new idea.

qa.q: How does Jin see the three unfinished projects?
qa.a: Jin notices the pattern kindly and says “None finished” without judging, but Jin may worry that Jamal is starting to see himself as someone who never finishes.

grounding: A teenager has several half-finished projects and a new idea feels more exciting, which builds a self-image as a non-finisher.

passage: The after-school club sign-up sheet went round again on Monday, and Ayesha wrote her name under Robotics. Indu, the coordinator, looked at the list. Ayesha had joined the chess club, the choir and the drama group since July, each for about three weeks. “I'm just a person who never finishes anything,” Ayesha said lightly, but her eyes stayed on the table. Indu didn't argue or give a speech. Indu asked, “Which one did you miss most after leaving?” Ayesha thought. “Chess. I liked the puzzle days.” Indu wrote “chess, term project: finish the ladder” in a small notebook and slid the notebook across. Ayesha looked at the page for a long moment, then crossed out Robotics.

qa.q: Which clubs had Ayesha joined since July?
qa.a: Ayesha had joined the chess club, the choir and the drama group.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's light tone and lowered eyes suggest she feels?
qa.a: Ayesha is hiding some hurt and shame under the light tone; the belief “never finishes anything” seems to weigh on Ayesha.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene makes Ayesha cross out Robotics?
qa.a: Indu asked which club Ayesha missed most, and Ayesha named chess, so a real interest replaced another new sign-up.

qa.q: What might Indu be thinking while writing in the notebook?
qa.a: Indu is probably gentle and hopeful, choosing a question over a lecture so Ayesha can arrive at the answer.

grounding: A teenager who has started and dropped many activities begins to see themselves as a non-finisher.

passage:
January. Lalit, fifteen, bought a second-hand guitar with his birthday money. For two weeks he practised every evening, fingertips sore and proud.
March. The guitar sat in the corner. Lalit had started an online coding course instead, because a friend had built a game. He finished four lessons of twenty. Then his cousin Kiran started running, and Lalit wrote a fitness plan on the wall.
May. Kiran asked, "How's the running?" Lalit looked at the guitar, the half-done course and the fading plan. "I'm just not a finisher," he said quietly. Kiran shook his head. "Pick one. Do it for a month. Just the boring bit." Lalit picked the guitar.

qa.q: How many lessons of the coding course did Lalit finish?
qa.a: He finished four lessons of twenty.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he said he was not a finisher?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and a bit ashamed, starting to see himself as someone who never completes things.

qa.q: What did Kiran suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Kiran suggested picking one project and doing the boring bit for a month, which gets Lalit through the dull stretch instead of jumping to something new.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Lalit's pile of half-finished projects?
qa.a: Kiran seems to see them as a habit Lalit can change, not a fixed trait, and pushes gently for one commitment.

grounding: Shows over months a teenager who starts a guitar, a coding course and a fitness plan without finishing any, and begins to see himself as a non-finisher.

passage: Francis, you remind me of your father Raghav when he was sixteen. Let me tell you. He had a harmonium, a stamp album and a book on carpentry, all started the same year. The harmonium he played for a month. The stamps filled three pages. The carpentry gave us one wobbly stool. Each time, he'd find something shinier. One evening I heard him tell his friend, "I'm the kind who never finishes." That worried me more than the unfinished things. So I asked him to finish just the stool, properly, with sanding and varnish. It took him six boring weeks. That stool is still in my kitchen.

qa.q: How many pages did Raghav's stamps fill?
qa.a: The stamps filled three pages.

qa.q: What worried the elder most about Raghav at sixteen?
qa.a: The elder was worried that Raghav had started calling himself the kind who never finishes, which was more troubling than the unfinished things.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Raghav?
qa.a: Being asked to finish just the stool properly, through six boring weeks of sanding and varnish, gave him one real completion.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when the stool was finally finished?
qa.a: Raghav might have felt proud and surprised, having proved to himself that he could get through the dull stretch.

grounding: An elder tells how a teenager began many projects, finished none and started to see himself as a non-finisher.

passage: Chinmay had one week before his school's talent show, and his room showed every plan he'd made that year: a keyboard with a missing key, a half-painted skateboard, a notebook titled "Learn Python" with three pages used. He'd signed up to play a keyboard piece, but it was only half learnt. His friend Varun, who was also performing, had a sprained wrist and couldn't practise with him. On Monday Chinmay felt the old itch to switch to a dance act instead. He sat on the bed, heart thumping. Then he taped the keyboard's broken key, set a daily half-hour and played the same eight bars until Friday. On Saturday he played the whole piece.

qa.q: How many pages of the Python notebook had Chinmay used?
qa.a: He had used three pages.

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel on Monday when he wanted to switch to dance?
qa.a: He felt anxious, with his heart thumping, tempted by the excitement of a new act over the dull practice.

qa.q: Which steps helped Chinmay finish, and why?
qa.a: Taping the broken key, setting a daily half-hour and repeating the same eight bars kept him going through the boring stretch.

qa.q: How might Varun feel watching Chinmay perform?
qa.a: Varun, unable to practise with a sprained wrist, might feel proud of Chinmay for finishing alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager with many half-finished projects pushing one through its dull stretch under time pressure.

passage:
In their flat in Mylapore, Ganga's shelf told the story. A half-knitted blue scarf on its needles since August. A coding course on her laptop, stuck at 40%. A skipping rope, and a fitness chart on the wall that stopped on day eleven.
On Saturday, she came in excited. "I'm going to learn calligraphy! Look, I found a pen set online."
Her brother Kishore, home from college, looked at the shelf, then at her. "What about the scarf?"
"It got boring. The middle part is just rows and rows."
"And the course?"
"Loops. So boring. Calligraphy is different."
He didn't laugh. "Ganga, you always say that. Everything is exciting on day one."
She opened her mouth to argue, then looked at the scarf. "Maybe I'm just someone who doesn't finish things."
"Or you've never finished one yet. Pick one. Just one."
She sighed, took down the scarf, and counted the rows left. Forty. "Four rows a day," she said. "Then calligraphy."

qa.q: How far had Ganga got in the coding course?
qa.a: Stuck at 40%.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when she looked at the scarf after Kishore's comment?
qa.a: Ganga felt doubtful and a little ashamed, wondering if she was someone who doesn't finish things.

qa.q: What plan does Ganga make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Four rows of the scarf a day before starting calligraphy, which makes the dull middle small and finishable.

qa.q: How does Kishore see Ganga's new calligraphy idea?
qa.a: Kishore sees it as the same pattern of exciting starts, but he responds kindly and nudges her to finish just one thing.

grounding: Shows a teenager with several half-finished projects who keeps chasing new excitement, until she chooses to push one through its dull stretch.
